41.0.0.en: 1 O death, how bitter is the remembrance of thee to a man that liveth at ease in peace among his possessions, 2 unto the man that hath nothing to vex him, that prospereth in all things, and is yet able to enjoy his food! 3 O death, acceptable is thy sentence unto the needy man, and him whose strength faileth, 4 that is now in old age, and is vexed with every care, that despaireth and hath lost patience! 5 Fear not the sentence of death. Remember thy former days and thy latter days; this is the sentence of the Lord over all flesh. 6 And why dost thou refuse that which is the good pleasure of the most High, whether it be ten years, or an hundred, or a thousand? 7 For in the grave there is no reckoning of life.

41.0.1.en: Ben Sira offers us a realistic picture of how people view death, before our thought was opened to the risen life that became ours through the resurrection of the Lord Christ. For the man who enjoys good health, who has authority and is well off and lives in security, looks upon death as cruel and bitter in taste, while the old man who suffers from sicknesses, frailty, and want looks upon it as a deliverance for him.

41.0.2.en: O death, how bitter is the remembrance of thee to the man who lives in peace with his possessions, to a man who is not distracted and prospers in everything, and is still strong enough to enjoy his food! [1]

41.0.3.en: When man concentrates on what befalls him, he looks upon life with a bitter eye. But when he lifts his heart to God, he sees in life a divine gift, and perceives God's plan behind the troubles that befall him, so his soul rejoices in a spirit of hope.

41.0.4.en: v Death is an exceedingly terrifying thing, but not for those who have learned the true wisdom that is from above. For he who knows nothing of the things to come, but counts death as dissolution and the end of life, rightly trembles and fears, as one passing into non-existence. But he who learns, by the grace of God, the hidden, secret things of the wisdom (of God), and counts it a departure to another place, finds no reason for trembling, but rather rejoices and is glad, since by leaving this perishable life we go to a better, more glorious life without end. This is what Christ teaches us by His actions, going to His sufferings not reluctantly or by necessity, but by His own will; therefore it is said: "When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples" [1].

41.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom O death, thy sentence is good for a needy man, weak in strength, who in his extreme old age (decrepitude) is distracted by everything, and becomes stubborn and lacking in patience [2].

41.1.1.en: Some look upon death as an escape from their financial, physical, psychological, and also spiritual troubles. David the psalmist cried out: "LORD, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him! or the son of man, that thou makest account of him! Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away" (Ps 144:3-4). Again he says: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" (Ps 8:4).

41.1.2.en: v Death is rest, deliverance from the dreadful toils and from the cares of the world [2].

41.2.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Fear not the sentence of death, and remember those who were before thee and those who come after [3].

41.2.1.en: If a man looks at those who preceded him, he finds no man on earth who escaped death, and if he looks at those who come after him, he finds that all know perfectly well that they will not live forever on earth. The wise man looks at those who preceded him, and sees the people of God in paradise sharing the praises of the heavenly ones, and their immortal life is blessed.

41.2.2.en: v Let the death of others stir you up, so that you may have a profitable fear and cast off all slackness, and let you examine your past works, cut off your sins, and begin a happy change [3].

41.2.3.en: v Consider to whom the departed one has gone, and be comforted. He has gone to where Paul and Peter are and the company of the saints. Consider how he will rise, with what glory and what exaltation. Consider that by your grief and lamentation you cannot change what has happened, and in the end you harm yourself.

41.2.4.en: St. John Chrysostom This is the sentence which the Lord has decreed over all flesh, so how will you resist the good pleasure of the Most High?

41.3.0.en: And in the grave there is no reckoning of your life, whether you lived ten years or a hundred or a thousand [4].

41.3.1.en: If the remembrance of death was exceedingly bitter for many in the ages before the coming of Christ, the One who rose from the dead said: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (Jn 11:25).

41.4.0.en: 8 The children of sinners are abominable children, and so are those who frequent the houses of the ungodly. 9 The inheritance of sinners' children shall perish, and reproach shall cleave to their posterity. 10 The children complain of an ungodly father, because they suffer reproach for his sake. 11 Woe unto you, ungodly men, which have forsaken the law of the most high God! 12 For if ye be born, ye are born to a curse: and when ye die, a curse is your portion. 13 All that are of the earth go to the earth: so the ungodly go from the curse to perdition. 14 Men mourn for their bodies, but the name of sinners shall be blotted out.

41.5.0.en: At the death of a man known to be wicked, the feeling of some people prevails that it is better to forget them, because remembering them is sometimes hateful. Some do not even want to think about them, for they do not deserve that anyone should remember them even in his thought for a moment, and this besides the eternal torment that the wicked meet. On the contrary, those of good reputation deserve to be remembered for a long time [12-13]. This is what moves the Church to hold yearly commemorations of the saints.

41.5.1.en: It is painful that the children of the wicked often walk in the way of their fathers, but the son who asks the Lord about the way of truth, the Lord grants him His grace, as happened with some kings such as the righteous Hezekiah, whose parents were wicked.

41.5.2.en: The children of sinners are abominable children, who often frequent the houses of the wicked [5].

41.5.3.en: Some may ask: Do all the children of the wicked walk in evil like their fathers? And what is their fault? The historical books, and history itself through the ages, answer these two questions, for the books highlighted the following:

41.5.4.en: a. Wicked kings who begot righteous sons. For example, King Hezekiah purified the land of Judah from the spread of idol worship and its abominations by the hand of his wicked father Ahaz. And Josiah, the last righteous king in Judah, did the same work to purify it from what his father Amon had done.

41.5.5.en: b. Wicked kings who begot wicked sons, such as Ahab and his wife the wicked Jezebel, who begot Ahaziah king of Israel, and he was wicked. It is often said of the wicked kings: "And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin" (1 Kgs 15:26).

41.5.6.en: c. Righteous kings who begot righteous sons, such as Asa king of Judah, who did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord and begot Jehoshaphat.

41.5.7.en: d. Righteous kings who begot wicked sons, such as David the prophet, who begot Absalom, who tried to seize the kingdom and kill his father.

41.5.8.en: These cases and the like confirm the personal responsibility of every man, so the Lord does not chastise the son for the sins of his father. "The soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ps 18:4, 20). As for his saying here: "The children of sinners are abominable children" [5], it is like the Lord's saying: "I visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me" (Deut 5:9). This does not mean that He visits them because of the guilt of the fathers, but He warns the fathers of the natural consequences, since the children from their childhood absorb the spirit of evil from their fathers, and often they go further in evil. As St. John Chrysostom says, the man who walks in evil recklessly does not care what befalls him, but he is often troubled when he feels that the fruit of what he does will return upon his children and grandchildren. It is as though God is calling them to repentance and to return to Him, if not out of fear of the bitter fruit of sin upon their own lives, then let them listen to Him in order to preserve their children and grandchildren.

41.5.9.en: St. John Chrysostom says that God threatens the wicked man, whether concerning himself or his children, not in order to carry out the punishment, but that he may turn back from his evil because of fear, as happened with the people of Nineveh, for He said that the city would perish because of their evils, and by saying this He made them resort to God's mercies by repentance instead of persisting in evil.

41.5.10.en: The inheritance of the children of sinners perishes, and shame cleaves to their offspring [6].

41.5.11.en: The children blame their wicked father, because on his account they are condemned [7].

41.5.12.en: Woe unto you, wicked men, for you have forsaken the law of the Most High God! [8]

41.5.13.en: The true secret of the destruction of the wicked is their forsaking of the Law, which is for the acquiring of wisdom and the enjoyment of righteousness.

41.5.14.en: v He who refuses to receive the light of the word of God ought to fear the punishment of the eternal darkness [4].

41.5.15.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles And when you were born, you were born to a curse, and when you die, the curse is your portion [9].

41.5.16.en: v This does not mean that God created them for destruction, but by their free will they made their life a curse and their death also a curse. The freedom of choice is declared to us through the Holy Scriptures not in human language but in divine. We begin with this truth, that if there were no freedom of choice, man would not use the commandments of God, and consequently would not receive the promised reward. He gives us the commandments so that no one can protest, excusing himself by his ignorance; therefore the Lord said in His Gospel of the Jews: "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloak for their sin" (Jn 15:22).

41.5.17.en: St. Augustine All that is of the earth returns to the earth, therefore the wicked go from the curse to perdition [10].

41.5.18.en: He who chose evil, what he chose returns upon him: the curse and destruction.

41.5.20.en: But the name of sinners is blotted out because it is not good [11].

41.5.21.en: While the wicked who persist in their stubbornness mourn for their bodies, which decay by death and rise on the day of the Lord to be recompensed for what they persisted in, behold, the people of God rejoice in hope even in the moments of death.

41.5.22.en: v Do not fear because you are burdened with a mortal body; let the Spirit be yours, and you will surely rise again... Truly all shall rise, but not all shall rise to life, but some shall rise to punishment and the others to life (Jn 29:5)...

41.5.23.en: He does not punish you if He sees His Spirit shining in you, but stops the punishment... and brings you into the bridal chamber to be there with the virgins (Mt 12:25). May you then not allow your body (the carnal life) to live in this world, so that your body may live there. Let it die that it may not die! For if you keep it alive here it does not live, but if it dies it lives. This is the state of the resurrection in general. For it must first die and be buried, and then it becomes immortal. But this takes place in the baptismal font, where the crucifixion and burial are accomplished and then the resurrection.

41.5.24.en: This also is what happened in the body of the Lord, for He was crucified and buried and rose. Let this also happen to us. Then we shall have the mortification of the works of the body, I do not mean the death of man's substance, for this is far from my intention, but the death of his inclinations toward evil things, for this too is life, indeed what is this but life [5].

41.6.0.en: 15 Have regard to thy name, for it shall continue with thee longer than a thousand great treasures of gold. 16 A good life hath but few days, but a good name endureth for ever. 17 Keep discipline in peace, my children, but wisdom that is hid, and a treasure that is buried, what profit is in them both?

41.6.1.en: Care for your name, for it endures with you more than a thousand great treasuries of gold [12].

41.6.2.en: A good life is a few numbered days, but a good name endures forever [13].

41.6.3.en: It is fitting that we bless God and thank Him, for He created us in His image and likeness. We cherish our name as human beings, for we fell but He did not leave us, but came down to us and granted us union with Him as members of His body.

41.6.4.en: v We become worthy to be called men when we are marked by reason; for if reason is not present we do not differ from the dumb animals except in the shape of the limbs and the gift of speech. Therefore let the reasonable man know that he is immortal, hating the shameful lusts which are the cause of the death of men [6].

41.6.5.en: St. Anthony the Great My children, observe the teaching, and live in peace.

41.6.6.en: But wisdom that is hid and a treasure that is unseen, what profit is in them both? [14]

41.6.7.en: The believer, by the Holy Spirit, is the voice of Christ crying out to men by every possible means that they prepare the way of the Lord and make His paths straight. This voice is the voice of self-giving love.

41.6.8.en: v A brother asked Abba Pimen: "If I see a brother about whom I have heard something evil, is it my duty not to let him into my cell? And if I see a good brother, am I to rejoice in him?" The Abba answered him: "If you do good to the good brother, do twice as much for that one, because he is sick."

41.7.s.en: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

41.7.0.en: 18 The man that hideth his foolishness is better than the man that hideth his wisdom. 19 Be ashamed of what I say unto you. 20 For it is not good to be ashamed of everything, neither is every thing done with discretion approved by every man. 21 Be ashamed of fornication before father and mother, and of a lie before the ruler and the mighty man. 22 Before the judge and the prince of an offence, and before the congregation and the people of iniquity. 23 Before a partner and friend of unjust dealing, and before the city where thou dwellest of theft. 24 And of transgressing the truth of God and his covenant; and of leaning with the elbow upon the bread; and of deceit in taking and giving. 25 And of silence before them that salute thee; and of looking upon a harlot. 26 And of turning away thy face from thy kinsman, and of taking away a portion and a gift. 27 And of gazing upon a woman that hath an husband, and of being overbusy with his maid, and by her bed thou shalt not stand. 28 And of upbraiding speeches before friends; and of grudging after thou hast given; and of repeating what thou hast heard and revealing what was said in secret.

41.7.1.en: The man who hides his foolishness is better than the man who hides his wisdom [15].

41.7.2.en: Sirach begins with an ironic contrast between the wise man and the fool. Ordinarily we expect from the wise man what is useful and beneficial, and from the fool what is ridiculous, but the case before us is unique, for the fool who hides his foolishness is better than the wise man who hides his wisdom. The first, by hiding his foolishness, has recognized his error, and has not exposed those around him to his foolishness. The second, when the Lord gave him wisdom, hid it, so he benefited neither himself nor his brethren [15]. The fool showed his wisdom by hiding his foolishness, and the wise man did not show love by revealing his wisdom. It was not fitting for the wise man to be ashamed of the wisdom the Lord gave him.

41.7.3.en: Sirach offers us a list of the things of which it is fitting for man to be ashamed. The purpose of this list is that society may not be lax in its principles and its evaluation of things, so that we do not feel ashamed of errors or evils which society, or the holy family, or the man of God must not accept. These shameful things come to about 20 items, and they are:

41.7.4.en: First: seven items concerning faults in speech or action:

41.7.5.en: a. Not discriminating in the kind of shame [16].

41.7.6.en: b. Speaking of fornication before one's parents [17].

41.7.7.en: c. Lying in the presence of the ruler or the leader [17].

41.7.8.en: d. Violating the law in the presence of the judge [18].

41.7.9.en: e. Committing iniquity before the congregation of the people [18].

41.8.0.en: f. Practicing injustice before your friend or your life partner [19].

41.8.1.en: g. Theft before a citizen in your country [19].

41.8.2.en: Second: four items concerning rashness and impropriety:

41.9.0.en: a. Neglecting the right of God and His covenant [20].

41.9.1.en: b. Breaking the manners of the table [20].

41.10.0.en: c. Showing disgust, whether in taking or in giving [21].

41.10.1.en: d. Silence before those who greet you [21].

41.10.2.en: Third: four items concerning shameful sexual matters:

41.11.0.en: a. An evil look at an evil woman [22].

41.11.1.en: b. Disregarding the entreaty of one of one's relatives [22].

41.12.0.en: c. Taking away someone's portion or gift [23].

41.12.1.en: d. Gazing at a married woman [23].

41.12.2.en: Fourth: four items concerning the disruption of friendship:

41.13.0.en: a. He who toys with his maidservant [24].

41.14.0.en: b. Being ashamed of insulting words directed to you in the presence of friends [25].

41.15.0.en: c. Insulting a person after giving him a gift [26].

41.15.1.en: d. Repeating words and revealing secrets [26].

41.15.2.en: Be ashamed, then, of the basis of my words, for it is not good to hold on to every kind of shame; not everything is highly esteemed with confidence by everyone [16].

41.15.3.en: The offenses of which one must always be ashamed are fornication, theft, unfaithfulness, iniquity, not honoring others, gossip, not dealing in taking and giving, silence before those who greet a person, gazing at an adulterous woman, ignoring the entreaty of relatives, toying with a maidservant (a nurse), insulting a friend, insulting one who offers him a gift, or repeating words and revealing a secret [16-27].

41.15.4.en: A man feels shame when he faces things which society does not accept, whether through an inherited tradition or things that touch the moral life. It is fitting for the young man to know how to evaluate this shame.

41.15.5.en: Be ashamed before your father and mother of fornication, and before your ruler or leader of lying [17].

41.15.6.en: Parents often want their children to be pure, so they cannot bear to hear that they practice fornication; indeed, they are not at ease even to hear about fornication from their children.

41.15.7.en: And before the judge of violating the law, and before the congregation of the people of iniquity [18].

41.15.8.en: Here he points to the courts that were set up at the gates of the city, which the judge and the elders of the city discussed together and in which they questioned the accused, and also heard the witnesses until they issued the verdict. From the origin of the Jewish synagogues during the Babylonian captivity until the middle of the twentieth century, if a Jew sinned publicly, the Jewish community would summon him before the council to declare his repentance publicly. And in the early Church confession was practiced publicly concerning what the penitent had done, especially concerning public sins.

41.15.9.en: And before your partner or friend of injustice, and before the place where you dwell of theft [19].

41.15.10.en: If a man practices injustice before his life partner (husband or wife) or before a friend, the life partner or the friend loses confidence in the one who did this, which causes troubles in family life or with friends.

41.15.11.en: Likewise, he who steals in the city where he lives, the people of the city keep away from him for fear that he may steal from them, so he feels that he is alone and rejected by society, and has no place in his city.

41.15.12.en: Be ashamed before the right of God and His covenant, and of evil conduct at the table [20].

41.15.13.en: Ben Sira links the one who commits a shameful thing in the house of the Lord, where he breaks his covenant with God, with the one who breaks the accepted rules of the table. For in the house of the Lord he is bound by the covenant with God so that the Lord may fulfill His promises to him, and at the table the peoples, especially in ancient times, used to consider eating together a kind of covenant between them, and no one may betray the covenant or lie or plot a conspiracy against the one who ate with him. This concept still prevails in the villages of Egypt, where a person says to his colleague: We have eaten bread and salt together, a sign of the commitment to behave with sincere love and faithfulness.

41.15.14.en: And of disgust in taking and giving, and of silence before those who greet you [21].

41.15.15.en: In offering help or a gift to a person, or in receiving help or a gift, it is fitting in both cases, in giving as in taking, to blend the conduct with kindness. For giving without love insults the recipient of the help or gift.

41.15.16.en: When someone greets a person, it is fitting for this person not to behave like one who is resentful of this greeting, which is a sign of peace and reconciliation (Mt 5:47).

41.15.17.en: And of looking at a harlot, and of refusing the entreaty of one of one's relatives [22]

41.15.18.en: With a spirit of discernment a man conducts himself, so that when he greets someone or someone greets him, his eyes must carry personal interest along with the greeting or salutation. And when he is in the presence of a woman along with an adulteress, it is not fitting for him to gaze at her or fix his eyes on her.

41.15.19.en: And of taking away someone's portion or gift, and of gazing at another man's wife [23].

41.15.20.en: And of meddling with his maidservant, and do not approach her bed [24].

41.15.21.en: The rich used to keep slaves and maidservants in their houses to serve them, under the system of slavery. And with the vast social difference, caution is needed, as Joseph the son of Jacob did, whom his mistress, the wife of Potiphar the captain of the guard, loved, and he fled from her.

41.15.22.en: And be ashamed of insulting speech before friends; after giving, do not insult the person [25]

41.15.23.en: When one of the relatives asks for something, one must not ignore him as far as possible. He who gives alms to a needy person and has not considered the feelings of the needy, spoils this giving which is without love!

41.15.24.en: And of repeating what has been heard, and revealing secrets [26].

41.15.25.en: Ben Sira has already spoken about the revealing of a secret, for it is almost impossible for a person to regain confidence in the one who revealed his secret.

41.16.0.en: Then you will feel true humility, and obtain favor before every man [27].

41.16.1.en: Sometimes when a man feels that he has been wronged, he finds it pleasant to rob the one who wronged him, and counts this a kind of reaction.

41.16.2.en: It is not permissible for a man to rob anyone secretly even if he has been wronged, but with courtesy and wisdom he should demand his right.

41.16.3.en: Sadly we sometimes hear that a person is negligent in his work on the plea that he works according to the amount paid to him. The element of faithfulness is vital; it is not permissible to be lax in it under any pretext.

41.16.4.en: Moreover, it is not permissible for the believer to gaze at a married woman, because he desires his brother's wife.

41.16.5.en: Here he links robbing the one who wronged him with gazing at his brother's wife, because both acts are secret theft. The first steals from the one who wronged him, and the second steals from his brother his wife through his looks.

41.16.6.en: Ben Sira concludes his twenty counsels concerning the things of which one must be ashamed by offering the remedy, which is that the believer be adorned with true humility, so that the grace of God may work in him and keep him from these shameful things!

41.17.s.en: Keep me from what is unseemly, and I will seek a speedy meeting with You

41.17.0.en: v Your divine presence turns the bitterness of death into sweetness as I pass through life in Your company!

41.17.1.en: I do not desire death in order to be delivered from the troubles of life!

41.17.2.en: But that I may pass over to You and live in Your embrace.

41.17.3.en: However long my life may be, it is like a single moment passing while I rejoice in You!

41.17.4.en: v Remove from me the roots of evil, lest the curse overtake me.

41.17.5.en: Your Law grants me wisdom, so I ask Your grace as my support.

41.17.6.en: I do not even disdain my body, for it shall rise and share in the glory of my soul.

41.17.7.en: What concerns me is the glory of Your holy name, for it is my great treasure!

41.17.8.en: I am bound to Your name, and so I enjoy my inner peace.

41.17.9.en: v Grant me the spirit of strength with discernment, that I may practice nothing of which I ought to be ashamed.

41.17.10.en: Let me honor my parents, and give honor to whom honor is due.

41.17.11.en: Let me not violate even the laws of the world, nor rob any man of his right.

41.17.12.en: I hold fast to Your covenant, so I enjoy the heavenly table.

41.17.13.en: May You sanctify my senses and my emotions and the movements of every member of my body.

41.17.14.en: I am careful to show personal interest in everyone as far as I can, and not to gaze at what it is not fitting for me to look upon.

41.17.15.en: Let my heart be a faithful treasury that does not reveal anyone's secret under any circumstance.

41.17.16.en: Grant me Your grace, that I may enjoy humility, which lifts me above all stumbling blocks, that I may soar in Your heavens!
